title: India is quietly doing great
gist: Noah Smith is more bullish on India than in a while (while bearish on China) because India's task is simpler: escape poverty and reach upper-middle income. He points to conquered extreme poverty with falling inequality, ~6.5% growth (Bloomberg sees 8% by decade-end), a 4x public-investment boom and broad-based manufacturing/export growth, while doubting The Economist's reform-and-macro-prudence explanation and flagging weak private investment and FDI as the key risk.

themes.theme: India bull vs. China bear: different tasks

insights.claim: Noah Smith is bearish on China's continued outperformance but more bullish on India than he has been in a while, because China is judged on eclipsing the US and allies or leading AI, whereas India only has to escape poverty and become upper-middle income.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supports overweighting India relative to China in EM allocations on a long-horizon development thesis.
insights.quote: India’s job right now is a lot simpler — it just has to escape poverty and become an upper middle income country
insights.locator: The reason I’m bullish on India

insights.claim: In both GDP and Human Development Index terms, India today is roughly where China was in the late 2000s, and its challenge is to make the infrastructure, jobs and technology leap China made in the 2010s.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Use China's 2010s build-out as a template for which Indian sectors (infrastructure, housing, energy) could boom.

insights.claim: Unlike China's industrialization, which the US wholeheartedly supported, India is industrializing despite China's attempts to throttle it by denying key technology exports and factory expertise.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: China export controls are a headwind for Indian manufacturing; easing or escalation would matter for India supply-chain plays.

insights.claim: Extreme poverty in India has mostly been conquered over the last two decades, and unlike China India achieved this while also reducing inequality.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Broad-based gains expand the domestic consumer base, favoring India consumption stories.
insights.quote: a full tenth of humanity saved from deprivation

insights.claim: The World Bank attributes India's poverty decline to strong consumption growth, rising employment especially among women, and expanded social transfers including food subsidies; Smith argues growth deserves the lion's share of credit.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Growth, not redistribution, is the main driver to monitor.
insights.locator: How did India manage this feat?

insights.claim: Since the pandemic India has grown faster than China, at about 6.5%, which nearly doubles living standards every decade, though slower than China's near-double-digit growth at a similar income level.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sustained ~6.5% real growth underpins long-run India earnings growth.
insights.quote: 6.5% is still a very healthy growth rate — it represents almost a doubling of living standards every decade
insights.locator: Now, India isn’t growing as fast

insights.claim: China only slowed to India's current growth rate in 2014, when it was 40% richer than India is now.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests India's growth is below China's comparable path, tempering the analogy.

insights.claim: Bloomberg expects Indian growth to accelerate to 8% by the end of the decade, and Neelkanth Mishra argues the incomplete pandemic recovery leaves plenty of room for acceleration.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Upside growth scenario for Indian equities and rupee assets.

insights.claim: The Economist credits India's growth to fiscal consolidation (deficit from 9.2% of GDP in fiscal 2021 toward a 4.4% target for fiscal 2026, ~0.9% excluding interest), 1.25 percentage points of rate cuts, inflation targeting, banking clean-up and reforms like cutting labour codes from 29 to four and lifting the 74% insurance FDI cap.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Fiscal and monetary easing room plus reforms are supportive of Indian bonds and financials.
insights.quote: A long-mooted cut in the number of labour codes, from 29 to four, was enacted in November.

insights.claim: India has opened nuclear power to the private sector and states are allowing women to work after dark, letting textile and electronics factories stay open later.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Opens private nuclear and extended-shift manufacturing opportunities.
insights.locator: Nuclear power has been opened up

insights.claim: Smith is skeptical that reforms and macro prudence explain the boom: long-term borrowing rates haven't fallen much, most structural reform is still in the future, and domestic private investment and FDI are not driving growth.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Watch private capex and FDI data; without a pickup the growth story rests on public spending.
insights.quote: I have to say, I’m skeptical of this story.
insights.locator: I have to say, I’m skeptical

insights.claim: Indian government investment has risen fourfold since before the pandemic despite falling debt levels, with highway spending up fivefold over a decade and central government railway spending up eightfold.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Direct tailwind for Indian infrastructure, construction, cement and capital-goods companies.
insights.quote: Highway spending has increased by a factor of five over the last decade. Central government railway spending has risen eightfold.
insights.locator: The Indian government has been on

insights.claim: The infrastructure boom lifts short-term growth and, longer term, will make both manufacturing and consumption much easier in India, including domestically built bullet trains such as the B28.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Infrastructure removes a chronic constraint, raising the ceiling for manufacturing FDI.
insights.locator: This is boosting growth in the

insights.claim: India's growth is broad-based, with manufacturing growing alongside services, overturning the old story that India leapfrogged manufacturing straight to outsourcing services.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: India is becoming a credible manufacturing alternative to China in supply-chain diversification.
insights.locator: The old story of India’s economy

insights.claim: Indian manufacturing output in August was 9% higher year on year, led by cars and electronics, and electronics exports rose 90% in dollar terms with US-bound iPhones a large share.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Apple's India supply chain and electronics manufacturers are key beneficiaries to track.
insights.quote: India’s electronics exports were up by 90% in August, year on year, with American-bound iPhones accounting for a large share of that

insights.claim: India's engineering exports are diversified: in FY 2025–26 automobiles were 21.9%, industrial machinery 18%, iron and steel 16.9%, other engineering 12.7%, electrical machinery 12.5% and non-ferrous metals 11.6%, unlike Bangladesh's garment-driven boom.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Diversification reduces single-sector risk in India's export story.

insights.claim: Whether India's boom continues past the next couple of years is an open question: private investment and probably FDI must rise, and rural education, female underemployment and incomplete urbanization must eventually be fixed.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Key watch items: private capex cycle and FDI inflows over the next 2 years.

insights.claim: Smith calls India perhaps the brightest economic success story in the world right now, less visible than China's rise but likely to be no less world-shaking.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Under-appreciated narrative implies potential for further re-rating as recognition grows.
insights.quote: perhaps the brightest in the entire world right now
